lesson_title: Whose Money Works Harder? Analysing a Company
hook_text: The shop borrows money at 8 percent and puts it to work earning 17,5. Who pockets the difference?
clip_script: Uncle Bongani wants the family to invest in his shop, and Aunt Nomsa — who trusts nobody's smile — asks for the books. Here is the question she cares about most. The shop's pot of long-term money is four million rand: the family's savings plus the bank's loan. Last year the business engine produced seven hundred thousand before anyone was paid — seventeen and a half cents on every rand in the pot. Now split the funders. The bank put in a million and charges eight percent: eighty thousand, good year or bad. The family gets everything that remains — fifteen percent on their money after tax. Sit with that: the shop borrows rands at eight cents and puts them to work earning seventeen and a half. Every borrowed rand WORKS FOR THE FAMILY. The bank does the funding; the family keeps the difference. That is gearing, and it is why sensible debt makes owners richer. But hear the other half. The bank's eighty thousand is owed in the bad years too. If the engine slowed to seven cents while the bank still wanted eight, every borrowed rand would start eating the family's dinner. Borrowed money is an amplifier — better good years, worse bad ones. And that one comparison — the engine's return against the cost of debt — is the heart of every analysis question in the paper.
visual_style: A money pot splitting into two labelled streams — bank and family — with coin-sized gears turning faster than the interest meter; the amplifier moment flips the scene dark as the gears slow and the interest meter keeps ticking.
mood: Sharp, kitchen-table practical, a little dramatic at the flip.
pacing: Steady build through the split, emphatic beat on who keeps the difference, ominous slowdown for the amplifier warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and argue any gearing, dividend or share-price question with confidence.
